legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Sakana Fugu Technical Report", Fugu Team, Sakana AI (team lead Yujin Tang; cite as "Sakana AI (2026)"). arXiv 2606.21228v2 [cs.LG], dated 2026-06-24 (v2 23 Jun 2026). Preprint, vendor tech report, not peer reviewed. The filename says tang-2026, but the printed author is "Fugu Team, Sakana AI".

COVERAGE: 100256 of 100256 chars read, including the references and Appendices A, B and C. Everything was read from the text extraction. The first 20k chars were read through a tool-result file, the rest in chunks. The sha1/latexit blobs from Figure 2 were filtered out as noise. Only the chart labels in Figures 5, 6, 8 and 10 are text; their visual content was not inspected.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Fugu-Ultra (RL-trained "Conductor") writes a natural-language workflow per query: subtasks, a worker id for each, and an access list saying which earlier outputs each worker sees. It reports SOTA on SWE-Bench Pro and Terminal Bench 2.1.
  number: SWE-Bench Pro 73.7 vs Opus 4.8 69.2, Gemini 54.2, GPT-5.5 58.6; Terminal Bench 2.1 82.1 vs GPT-5.5 78.2, Opus 74.6
  setup: pool is Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-Opus-4.8 and GPT-5.5. Minimal harnesses (Mini-SWE-agent, Terminus 2). Baselines are mostly provider-reported, "with the same maximum reasoning effort configured".
  quote: "Fugu-Ultra excels in agentic coding and software engineering, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both SWE Bench Pro and Terminal Bench 2.1... both in the range of 5-6% relative to the next best performer"
  where: section 4.1.2 and Table 1, p.10-11
- The single-selection Fugu (Trinity-based) picks one worker per input with a head on the orchestrator's hidden state. It still beats the best single worker on Terminal Bench.
  number: Fugu 80.2 on Terminal Bench 2.1 vs GPT-5.5 78.2; Fugu 92.9 on LiveCodeBench vs 88.5 best baseline; SWE Pro only 59.0
  setup: one worker per input, latency "comparable to a direct call". The trajectories show per-step switching between GPT-5.5 and Opus.
  quote: "Despite Fugu only selecting one model for each input, we find that Fugu can also substantially outperform the state-of-the-art GPT-5.5 in this task."
  where: 4.1.2, p.11
- Fugu's parametrization is decision-only. A lightweight head outputs L logits, one per worker, read from the hidden state at an early token, so there is no autoregressive decoding. It has no role assignment, unlike Trinity. Only the head and the singular-value scales of selected matrices are trained (SVF, from Transformer-squared).
  quote: "Removing role assignment narrows the coordination space to model selection alone, which keeps the orchestration decision simple and minimizes the latency overhead of the orchestrator."
  where: 3.1.1, p.5-6
- Fugu training has two stages.
  1. SFT on single-step verifiable tasks. The target is a softmax over each worker's mean reward, p_i(j)=exp(r̄_ij/τ)/Σ exp(r̄_ij'/τ). The loss is KL against the head's distribution.
  2. sep-CMA-ES on end-to-end multi-turn trajectories from Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, with a terminal reward in {0,1}. This is "substantially more stable than supervised fine-tuning" on those tasks.
  number: none (no ablation reported)
  where: 3.1.2-3.1.3, p.6-7
- Fugu-Ultra reward and training: reward is 0 if the workflow is unparseable, 1 if the final answer is correct, and 0.5 for a well-formed but wrong workflow. Trained with GRPO and no KL penalty. Workflows are capped at 5 steps. The orchestrator can itself be a worker.
  quote: "Ultra is instructed to design agentic workflows of up to 5 steps"; "We train using our Conductor reward detailed in section 3.2.1 with GRPO and without any KL divergence penalty."
  where: 3.2.1, 3.2.3, p.8-9
- Multi-agent function calling needs two memory rules. Intra-workflow agent isolation: each agent sees only its own tool trajectory, and sees others only via the access list. Without it, "orchestration collapse" follows. Persistent shared memory across workflows: agents see earlier workflows' tool calls to avoid redundant calls. The orchestrator also tracks workflow state (which agent emitted each call, the topology, the subtasks).
  quote: "orchestration collapse, whereby the first agent to interact with the environment sets the trajectory for all future agents, leading to redundant contributions from future agents"
  where: 3.2.2, p.8-9
  number: none (qualitative, no ablation)
- Learned topologies observed, all as anecdotes from single trajectories.
  - Tree with a dynamically chosen aggregator: Gemini aggregates trivia (HLE Heroes of Might & Magic III), GPT aggregates math (Crowley-Nordström invariant). Two leaf agents work independently.
  - Build-and-debug: GPT builds, Opus reviews and finds the issues (PyPI server task).
  - Lead engineer plus clean-slate second opinion: Opus leads, GPT re-examines (SWE-Bench Pro gravitational/teleport).
  - Specialist handoff: Opus writes the attack, GPT re-derives the maths (FEAL cryptanalysis).
  - The authors say other multi-agent systems fix one model as the final synthesizer.
  quote: "dynamic adaptation of an aggregator role is precisely the kind of adaptation unavailable to existing multi-agent systems (OpenRouter, Inc., 2026; Wang et al., 2025), which necessitate a fixed model to always act as a final synthesizer"
  where: 4.4, p.16-18
  number: none
- Routing adapts by domain. Both variants peak on GPT-5.5 for Terminal Bench and on Gemini for GPQA-Diamond, and Ultra is balanced across three agents on HLE. Math goes mostly to GPT, chemistry and biology to Gemini.
  quote: "in GPQA-Diamond, where Gemini-3.1-Pro is the leading model, both Fugu models focus their orchestration around Gemini."
  where: 4.2 and Figure 5, p.12-13
  number: none (the distribution values are only in the figure)
- Other Table 1 results. GPQA-D 95.5 for both Fugu variants vs Gemini 94.3. LiveCodeBench Ultra 93.2 vs 88.5 best baseline. Fugu-Ultra beats the unavailable Mythos Preview and Fable 5 on GPQA, CharXiv and Terminal Bench (Fig 4).
  quote: "intelligent orchestration ought to be an additional axis to scale performance without scaling training compute."
  where: 4.1.3, p.11
- Orchestration does not always win. Fugu-Ultra trails on SciCode 58.7 vs Gemini 58.9, and Fugu scores 60.1 there. On MRCRv2 Ultra gets 93.6 vs GPT-5.5 94.8. On Long Context Reasoning Ultra gets 73.3 vs GPT-5.5 74.3. On τ3 Banking Fugu-Ultra scores 20.6, equal to Opus and GPT. Fugu scores 21.7.
  where: Table 1, p.11
- AutoResearch (123 experiments, ~14h per seed, single H100, 3 seeds): Fugu-Ultra scores 0.9774±0.0019 mean BPB vs the best single model's 0.9781±0.0011. The gap is within about one std.
  quote: "These gains are modest in absolute magnitude, as expected for a highly optimized training pipeline"
  where: 4.3.1, Table 2, p.14
- Reading-order task, 25 expert pages, same beam search for all models: Fugu-Ultra scores 0.776 NED vs 0.642 for the best frontier model, Fugu 0.473 and a seed heuristic 0.116. One frontier model did not complete the run. This one was constructed by the authors.
  where: 4.3.2, Table 3, p.16
- Appendix B tasks, which are illustrative and mostly show Fugu-Ultra near or above the best single model.
  - Rubik's solver, 300 cubes: Ultra scores 19.72 HTM vs Model A 19.76, and two baselines crash on all 300. Fugu scores 21.15 HTM at 1.9 s per cube.
  - Blindfold chess: 4 games, all wins, selected games and "not an aggregate or a win rate".
  - Stock trading, 5 runs, one anonymized equity, 50 weeks: Ultra reaches +19.43% (±$633.86) and baselines are under +15%. The authors caveat that "Results may not transfer to other assets, time periods, or live markets."
  where: App. B, p.27-30

LIMITS
- No ablations. There is no test of isolation vs shared context, orchestrator vs best-of-N or fixed debate, topology vs the same models run independently, SFT vs ES, or the RL reward design.
- No cost, latency or token numbers for Ultra. It "trades additional latency", but none are reported. The Fugu latency claim is also unquantified.
- Baselines are mostly provider-reported or third-party leaderboard numbers, not rerun under one harness. Mythos and Fable 5 are not in the pool and "max of the two" is used.
- The pool is only three closed frontier models. The orchestrator and backbone are not named, and weights are not released as far as I could tell. There are no seeds or error bars on the benchmarks. The three Model A/B/C baselines are anonymized and the mapping varies across examples.
- The topology findings are cherry-picked qualitative anecdotes. The per-topology frequency and win rate are not given. The "no pre-defined topology" claim has no comparison against fixed topologies.
- The text and Table 1 do not agree on HLE. The Figure 1 chart labels read 50.0 / 48.5 / 53.3 for Ultra, Fugu and Fable 5, but the Table 1 HLE row has Fugu at 47.2 and Opus at 49.8. I could not resolve which is current, so check before citing.
- The word "SOTA" is claimed against publicly accessible models only. Fable 5 and Mythos Preview are not accessible.
- Several numbers are only in figures: the Figure 5 distributions, the Figure 6 curves, and the Figure 10 baseline values.
- Dated: the model names (GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro) and benchmark versions are mid-2026.

BUILDS ON
- Trinity: Xu et al., arXiv 2512.04695, 2025. Evolved LLM coordinator, sep-CMA-ES. Basis of Fugu.
- Conductor: Nielsen et al., arXiv 2512.04388, 2025. RL-trained workflow orchestrator. Basis of Fugu-Ultra.
- GRPO: Shao et al. (DeepSeekMath), arXiv 2402.03300, 2024.
- Singular-value fine-tuning: Sun et al., "Transformer-squared", ICLR 2025.
- Mixture-of-Agents: Wang et al., ICLR 2025.
- Multiagent debate: Du et al., ICML 2024.
- GPTSwarm (agents as optimizable graphs): Zhuge et al., ICML 2024.
- MasRouter: Yue et al., arXiv 2502.11133, 2025.
- RouterDC: Chen et al., NeurIPS 2024.
- Smoothie: Guha et al., NeurIPS 2024.
- Multi-agent evolving orchestration: Dang et al., arXiv 2505.19591, 2025.
- Automated Design of Agentic Systems: Hu et al., ICLR 2025.
- Evolutionary model merging: Akiba et al., Nature Machine Intelligence 2025.
- Also cited: CoT (Wei et al., 2022), ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, Self-Refine, Reflexion, and the OpenRouter Fusion comparison.

CODE: No code. The pseudo-structure is a workflow step = (subtask string, worker id, access list of earlier step indices). Equations (1)-(5) are the SFT softmax target and the ES update. The reward rule is in 3.2.1.

FIGURES
- Figure 2 (p.5), Fugu parametrization. A selection head runs parallel to the LM head, taking a hidden state to L worker logits, with no roles. It shows decision-only routing faster than prose.
- Figure 5 (p.13), per-task model distribution. It shows the routing adapting by domain, but the values are only in the figure.
- Figure 1 (p.2), benchmark bars. It is cluttered, and its HLE labels disagree with Table 1.
- Best single candidate: Figure 2, if the note is about orchestrator design. If the note is about topology, no figure shows a topology, so none is worth taking. Table 1 is the useful artifact.

FIT
- Best fit is 05-topology-patterns.md. It gives a learned, query-adaptive topology (chain, tree and best-of-N, with the aggregator chosen per query) and evidence against a fixed aggregator.
- It also bears on isolation vs shared state. The "orchestration collapse" and the intra-workflow isolation plus persistent memory split are about shared state and the access list as a graph edge definition. If a state or memory note exists in the folder, this fits there too.
- Check the notes folder for a router/selection note. The single-worker Fugu variant is routing, not topology.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean text. The PDF has no embedded instructions. Figure 2 contained long latexit base64 blobs, which were discarded. The Figure 1 chart labels are scrambled in order, so Figure 1 per-model values are ambiguous. Table 1 is the reliable source. Tool outputs were truncated in places, and the text was re-read from the saved extraction at /tmp/fugu.txt.
